name: Union of Concerned Scientists: global security and science and democracy (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: almost all the value is the nuclear-weapons work, against a risk that kills people everywhere, so the result is spread by world population; the science-and-democracy work (under 1% of the value) is for Americans.
summary: The Union of Concerned Scientists (Cambridge, Massachusetts) uses technical analysis and advocacy against the risk of nuclear war (its Global Security programme: the Sentinel missile, plutonium pits, missile defence, nuclear testing) and, through its Center for Science and Democracy, for independent federal science and its use in policy; this model covers those two programmes in the year to September 2025 ($11.9M with overhead; its climate, transport and food work is a separate model). At the defaults it averts about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, from {{low}} to {{high}} on its plausible range: almost all of it the nuclear work ({{row:nuclear_cost_share}} of the cost), valued as a typical project's cut in the forecast risk of nuclear war (Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's experts), with deaths valued like every death and the future lost counted only where you count lives that never start (0% by default); the science-and-democracy work, valued as better use of US public money, adds under 0.01%. Only half the spending here is on nuclear risk, and its net assets of about 17 months of spending make the next dollar count for less. The biggest uncertainty is how much a dollar of such work cuts the risk (Rethink calls its figures placeholders; the range runs ten times either way); the result also moves with the years a cut counts and the discount rate. Every branch is discounted for missing data: no outcome of the work is measured.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

rows.label: Science and democracy: public money a year in the programmes the work touches, per dollar spent
rows.explainer: The yearly public budgets whose use a dollar of the work bears on: the federal science agencies whose research and rules it defends (among them NOAA, whose climate research it campaigned to keep in 2025, annual report p. 4), the rules whose science it tracks (402 attacks on science in six months, by its count, p. 6) and public comment on federal rulemaking. The agencies' budgets run to billions a year, but each campaign touches a part of them and many groups press on the same lines: 100 dollars of public money a year per dollar of the work, from 10 to 1,000, our judgment with no reference class.

rows.label: Share of public investment's value lost to inefficiency, advanced economies
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how much better public spending in rich countries could do (the IMF's efficiency gap for public investment, facts/democracy.json): the room the work can close. It is measured on investment and applied here to all the public spending the work touches, programmes and regulation too, for want of a figure for those; gov_gap_closed's wide range covers the difference.

rows.label: Science and democracy: share of that gap the work closes in the programmes it touches, a year
rows.explainer: Most of the work defends science against cuts and distortion and moves a rule or a budget line only with many others, so it closes a small part of the gap: 2% (0.2% to 10%), our judgment.

rows.label: Value of a dollar of US public good, in units of value
rows.explainer: A dollar more of what public money buys for Americans, valued like a dollar of consumption to the average American: one over the household survey's consumption per person (the Consumer Expenditure Survey, 2024, in 2025 dollars: the one scale for US public money, docs/normalization.md 2.14) in ln(consumption), × the shared value of doubling consumption. No marginal cost of public funds: better use of the same money costs the payers nothing more.

rows.formula: cost_total * gov_cost_share * gov_public_dollars_per_dollar * gov_efficiency_gap * gov_gap_closed * gov_discounted_years * gov_value_per_public_dollar
rows.explainer: The branch's cost × public money touched per dollar × the share of its value lost to inefficiency × the share of that the work closes × the discounted years × the value of a dollar of US public good. Enters the result through the bridge from units of value (uov_bridged).

rows.formula: -((cost_total * ai_cost_share / 1e6 * ai_future_per_million * ai_discounted_years) + (cost_total * bio_cost_share / 1e6 * bio_future_per_million * bio_discounted_years) + (cost_total * nuclear_cost_share / 1e6 * nuclear_future_per_million * nuclear_discounted_years) + (pol_wins * pol_p_success * pol_relative_cut * pol_future_per_year * pol_discounted_years) + (fb_work_dollars / 1e6 * fb_credit_share * fb_future_per_million * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, years_of_impact))) * $lives_added * $animal_dalys_per_person_year_world
rows.explainer: A future kept is also every animal raised to feed it: each future person-year at the suffering of the animals an average person eats in a year today (docs/normalization.md 2.25). Suffering always counts, whatever lives that never start count; the farmed animals' own good days count where you set them to. Held at today's diet: no forecast of what people will eat is used.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Whether UCS's other funders (foundations, about 13% of its donor revenue) would give less if small donors gave more is the room factor of @next_dollar.union_of_concerned_scientists (docs/normalization.md 2.10), so it isn't asked again here (one question per adjustment): 1, our judgment, as for every catastrophic-risk model; 0.85 to 1.05 for funging the room factor misses.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: no outcome of UCS's work is measured, on the risk (a typical project's cut and forecast chances) or on public spending (the gov branch's chain is judged), so the shared missing-data step applies to every branch (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Good beyond what is counted, each part a share of the modelled value (almost all the nuclear branch's): work against a single detonation or a limited nuclear war (the testing moratorium, the Korean peninsula), which kills far fewer than 10% of people and has no shared forecast (nuclear_smaller_per_year 0), 6%; the 2025 expansion of the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act (about $8 billion for some 125,000 more people, annual report p. 12), whose value is the transfer to ill and often poorer recipients less its cost to taxpayers, at roughly a dollar of consumption to the average American per dollar paid, UCS one of several groups behind five years of work, 1%. 7% (0 to 25%) in all, our judgment. The Center for Science and Democracy's election and environmental-justice work is left in the gov branch's wide range (gov_gap_closed), not added here: a share of this total would credit it hundreds of times its own branch.

rows.label: Harm: speeding up dangerous capabilities, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: A typical project's chance of backfiring is already in the shared cut per dollar (Rethink Priorities' backfire step). Analysis and advocacy on nuclear weapons can't speed up any capability. 0, down to -5%, our judgment.

rows.label: Harm: information hazards and attention, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire (in the shared cut): advocacy against new US weapons could, some argue, weaken deterrence; none is shown to happen, and UCS publishes no technical weapons detail beyond what governments release. 0, down to -5%, our judgment.
